## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1 (God "remembered")**
- Guzik says "remembered" is a human way of describing God. God never forgot Noah. He sustain[ed] him every day on the ark. But at this point, God again turned His active attention towards Noah. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-8/
- The Hebrew word *zakar* means more than recalling. When God "remembers" us, He acts for us. Zakar also means to act on a person's behalf. Precept Austin adds that God is acting on His earlier promise in 6:18. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-8-commentary
- Gill says God remembered His covenant and promise to keep everyone in the ark alive. He notes the Targums call the wind "a wind of mercies", or a merciful wind. Matthew Henry says God remembering Noah was the return of his mercy to mankind, of whom he would not make a full end. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/8-1.htm
- Calvin points out that God could have dried the earth by unseen power but chose to use wind, which method he also employed in drying the Red Sea. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/8-1.html
- The word for wind (*ruach*) is the same one used for God's Spirit hovering over the waters in Genesis 1:2. Some take this as a hint of new creation. — https://biblehub.com/study/genesis/8-1.htm

**v. 4 (Ararat)**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the ark really ran aground; it did not just stop drifting. "Mountains" means one of the mountains. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/8-4.htm
- Barnes says Ararat was a country, not a mountain. He doubts the ark landed on either of the peaks now called Ararat. — same URL
- Clarke says no one can know where in the range the ark rested, and these things are certainly of very little consequence. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/genesis/8-4.html
- **The date:** Ellicott and Pulpit cite the Speaker's Commentary. It counts the seventh month as Abib, which makes the date the same day as the Red Sea crossing and Christ's resurrection. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/8-4.htm
- One Bible Hub study note disagrees and calls the seventh month Tishri. The two calendars conflict, so treat the resurrection link with care. — https://biblehub.com/study/genesis/8-4.htm

**v. 5 (mountain tops seen)**
- Guzik takes this as further evidence that the flood was worldwide. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-8/
- Ellicott thinks "seen" means the peaks became clearly visible as mist and vapour lifted, not that they were only just emerging. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/8-4.htm

**vv. 6–7 (window, raven)**
- Guzik says the raven, a scavenger, probably rested and fed on floating carcasses. Quoting Spurgeon: "True faith often goes to the window." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-8/
- Matthew Henry reads the Hebrew "going forth and returning" to mean the raven perched *on* the ark, probably not in it. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_008.cfm
- Calvin thinks Noah chose a raven on purpose, because carcasses would draw it further out if land were exposed. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/8-6.html

**vv. 8–9 (dove returns)**
- Guzik says the dove, a clean bird that doesn't scavenge, would not land until there was a fit place. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-8/
- Henry turns Noah drawing the dove back in into a picture of Christ. Just as Noah took the dove in, so Christ will graciously preserve, and help, and welcome, those that fly to him for rest. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/8-8.html

**vv. 10–11 (olive leaf)**
- The leaf showed the waters were down to the level where olives grow and that life was returning. The Cambridge Bible notes the scene finds no counterpart in the Babylonian story. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/8-11.htm
- Barnes cites ancient writers who say the olive strikes leaves even under water. — same URL
- Calvin also notes olives don't grow on mountains, so the leaf showed that fruitful lowlands were clear. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/8-6.html
- Spurgeon complains that pictures show a branch when It was an olive leaf, that is all. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-8-commentary
- Henry Morris (a creationist) says seeds and cuttings buried in flood sediment could sprout quickly. Precept Austin instead suggests God supernaturally made the plants sprout. — same URL

**v. 12 (dove does not return)**
- Guzik: the dove staying away proved the earth could be lived on again. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-8/
- Henry and Benson suggest the seven-day gaps may mean Noah kept the Sabbath. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/8-8.html

**vv. 15–17 (come out, be fruitful)**
- Guzik notes the family was in the ark about a full calendar year. He also notes the text mentions no animal deaths aboard. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-8/
- Quoting Spurgeon: God told Noah when to go in but not when he would come out, because Noah didn't need to know that. — same URL

**v. 20 (altar, sacrifice)**
- Guzik: Noah's first act was worship. With only seven of each clean animal, the sacrifice was costly. He ties it to Romans 12:1 and David's refusal to offer what cost him nothing (2 Samuel 24:24). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-8/

**v. 21 (pleasing aroma, "evil from youth")**
- Ellicott says the point is not so much that the sacrifice gave God pleasure as that it caused Him to regard man with complacency. The anger at sin which had caused the flood was now over. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/8-21.htm
- Guzik says God was more pleased by Noah's heart than by the smell itself. Quoting Spurgeon, he calls the sacrifice "the turning-point," a picture of Christ's atonement. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-8/
- **"For" or "although"?** Benson says the Hebrew word can be translated "although," meaning God spares the earth *although* He has good reason not to. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/8-21.htm
- Coffman says reading it as the *reason* for the promise is a mistake. The point is that Noah's descendants will be no better than Adam's. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/8-21.html

**v. 22 (seasons)**
- Guzik links the seasons to the end of a "covering of water vapors" (the vapour-canopy theory). He also links them to shorter lifespans and an ice age after the flood. This is a disputed young-earth view. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-8/
- Maclaren says God works to draw people to repentance by the faithful continuance of His beneficence in the steadfast covenant of revolving seasons. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/8-1.htm

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

There was no clear denominational split in what I read. The differences below are in emphasis and method.

- **v. 21, sin from birth.** Calvin (Reformed): "from youth" shows that men are born evil, and philosophers wrongly put down to habit what God puts down to nature. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/8-21.html
- Gill (Baptist) also says sin is sinful, and that originally, even from his birth. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n95/genesis/8-21.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist) preached a whole sermon on this verse, linking human depravity with God's covenant mercy. — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/human-depravity-and-divine-mercy
- **vv. 6–12, how far to take the allegory.** Calvin warns against futile allegories. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/8-6.html
- Henry passes on, as something "some" say, that the raven stands for the Law and the dove for the Gospel. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_008.cfm
- Lutheran writing on 1517.org uses the same two birds for its Law and Gospel framework: From the pulpit flies forth the dove of the Gospel. — https://www.1517.org/articles/birds-in-the-pulpit
- Gaebelein (dispensationalist) reads the dove's flights as stages in the Holy Spirit's work. The first, finding no rest, is the Old Testament period; the second is the present age. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/8-8.html
- **Baptism (Lutheran).** 1517.org collects Church Fathers who see the flood as a picture of baptism, with the dove as the Spirit coming to the believer at the font. — https://www.1517.org/articles/baptism-foreshadowed-in-old-testament-narratives

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship** (found only in older critical commentaries on Bible Hub)
- **v. 4:** The Cambridge Bible says Ararat is the region known in Assyrian inscriptions as "Urartu." It suggests the familiar name may have replaced a less-known name of hills near the Tigris. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/8-4.htm
- **v. 21:** Ellicott mentions the source theory (different authors called the Jehovist and Elohist) and the charge that this verse contradicts 6:5. He answers that the Bible often states both sides of a principle bluntly. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/8-21.htm

**Catholic**
- **vv. 6–12:** Ambrose reads the scene as a picture of baptism. The water washes sin away, the wood of the ark is the cross, the dove is the Holy Spirit, and The raven is the figure of sin, which goes forth and does not return. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3405.htm
- Augustine says that if the ark is a figure of the Church, the Church must hold both ravens (those who seek their own) and doves. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701006.htm
- The Catholic Encyclopedia says the dove became a symbol of peace from this story. Early Christian art showed the faithful as doves entering the Ark of God, the Church. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02576b.htm
- **v. 21:** The Catholic Douay-Rheims translation softens the wording to "prone to evil." — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n95/genesis/8-21.html
